newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece faces wave of strikes over stiff budget.
newsitem.headline: Greece faces wave of strikes over stiff budget.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis returns from Dublin's European Union summit on Sunday to a week of strikes against his tough budget.

Farmers, who have blocked national roads for 18 days, are threatening to drive their tractors into Athens while the capital's public servants, teachers, doctors and diplomats say they will strike during the five-day parliamentary debate on the budget starting on Tuesday.
The 1997 budget, designed to qualify Greece to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 2001, cuts state hiring, abolishes most tax exemptions and imposes new taxes.
Simitis, who has described the budget as the harshest in 15 years, has said "no" to any workers' group asking for more money. Reaction is growing even within his government.

For the first time since winning elections in September he is accused by labour unions of being arrogant and indifferent to the problems of the average Greek, and a "Brussels servant" by the opposition press.
"We should not base our national policy on the blackmail: Maastricht or catastrophe," said Simitis's education minister Gerassimos Arsenis. "The people can't be motivated by such dillemas."

On Monday Simitis was expected to hold his third special cabinet meeting in two weeks to face the farmers' revolt. Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos, the government's number two, urged him to meet with the farmers and discuss their problems.

Pressing for cheaper fuel and state subsidies for their products, the farmers have set up five blocks with thousands of tractors along the main north-south highway and vow to continue the seizure over the Christamas holidays.
The blockade, in its third week, has caused millions of dollars in damages to industry, hoteliers and export companies but Simitis has rejected all calls for compromise.
"If you satisfy the demands of one group then you have to satisfy the demands of everybody else as well, and this will simply destroy the economy," a senior government official told Reuters.
A staunch pro-European professor, Simitis has said sacrifices are needed to converge the Greek economy with those of its EU partners.
The budget, which goes on vote in parliament next Saturday, will yield the state next year about $4 billion from the extra taxes and spending cuts.

"The vote on the budget is seen as a vote of confidence to the government. The prime minister has made this clear to all our deputies in parliament. The economic policy is one way towards Europe," the government official said.
The country's two biggest labour confederations have called a one-day nationwide strike on Tuesday and smaller strikes with daily marches to parliament scheduled throughout the week.
The streets of Athens echo daily from the chants of unhappy civil workers, pensioners, students, and customs employees protesting against the tight incomes policy.
Even diplomats, the most loyal of civil servants, have joined the strikes to protest against a new tax on an allowance given to diplomats abroad to cover living and travelling costs.
